reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: Caused by autoantibodies against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, present in both the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes
Classically presents as a pulmonary-renal syndrome with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and alveolar haemorrhage, though isolated renal disease is common
Renal presentation is a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with haematuria, red-cell casts and often oliguric acute kidney injury
Biopsy shows diffuse crescentic glomerulonephritis, and immunofluorescence demonstrates the hallmark smooth linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
A subset are double-positive for ANCA (usually anti-MPO), which alters relapse risk and management
It is a medical emergency: outcome depends on prompt plasma exchange to remove circulating antibody combined with immunosuppression/corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide
Pulmonary haemorrhage is precipitated or worsened by smoking, infection and fluid overload
reference.pathophysiology: Anti-GBM disease is an autoimmune small-vessel vasculitis in which circulating IgG autoantibodies bind a conformational epitope on the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen (the Goodpasture antigen) within basement membranes. Antibody binding along the glomerular basement membrane activates complement and recruits neutrophils and macrophages, causing capillary wall rupture, fibrinoid necrosis and crescent formation, hence the linear IgG staining and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The same antigen in alveolar capillary basement membranes is normally shielded, but injury from smoking, infection or inhaled toxins exposes it, allowing antibody-mediated alveolar haemorrhage. Loss of self-tolerance to the sequestered epitope, often on a permissive HLA background, initiates the process.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of diffuse alveolar haemorrhage such as severe infection or cardiac failure
additionalInvestigations: Serum anti-GBM antibody testing by ELISA
ANCA (anti-MPO and anti-PR3) to detect double-positive disease
Urgent renal biopsy showing crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG on immunofluorescence
Chest imaging and assessment of gas transfer for alveolar haemorrhage
Full blood count, renal function and urinalysis with microscopy for red-cell casts
Complement studies and lupus serology to exclude alternative causes
redFlags: Massive or worsening pulmonary haemorrhage with hypoxia
Oliguric acute kidney injury or dialysis dependence at presentation
High proportion of glomeruli with crescents on biopsy
Delay in diagnosis, as irreversible renal failure develops quickly
reference.prognosis: Prognosis hinges on early treatment: patients treated before advanced renal failure often preserve kidney function, whereas those who are oliguric or dialysis-dependent with extensive crescents rarely recover renal function despite therapy. Pulmonary haemorrhage responds better to treatment than established renal failure, and disease relapse is uncommon except in double-positive (ANCA) patients.
pitfalls: Delaying plasma exchange and immunosuppression while awaiting biopsy in a rapidly progressive presentation
Missing coexisting ANCA positivity that changes relapse risk and monitoring
Attributing alveolar haemorrhage to infection alone and overlooking the renal component
Assuming irreversibility without a biopsy to gauge the balance of active crescents versus fibrosis
Under-appreciating smoking and infection as triggers of pulmonary bleeding
management: Urgent plasma exchange to remove circulating anti-GBM antibody as the cornerstone of treatment
Immunosuppression with corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide to suppress antibody production
Renal replacement therapy for severe acute kidney injury while awaiting response
Treat life-threatening alveolar haemorrhage with intensified plasma exchange and respiratory support, and encourage smoking cessation to reduce recurrent pulmonary bleeding
Monitor anti-GBM antibody titres to guide treatment duration and defer renal transplantation until antibodies are undetectable
Add maintenance immunosuppression for ANCA double-positive disease given the higher relapse risk, with nephrology follow-up
